title: India's Satluj Controversy Exposes Growing Fear of Censorship Among Bollywood Filmmakers
excerpt: The removal of Diljit Dosanjh's film from ZEE5 within 48 hours has reignited a national debate over creative freedom, OTT regulation, and the boundaries of storytelling in Indian cinema.
body:
• Diljit Dosanjh's Satluj was removed from ZEE5 within 48 hours of its July 3 premiere after a government directive citing national security concerns.
  • The film, based on slain Punjab human rights activist Jaswant Singh Khalra, spent three years battling censors who demanded nearly 100 cuts under its original title Punjab 95.
  • A PIL challenging the ban was filed in the Punjab and Haryana High Court, which declined to hear it but noted it was "not averse to judicial review."
  • The controversy has triggered broader industry anxiety about self-censorship, with filmmakers and actors divided on whether to fight the ban through courts or public campaigns.

When Diljit Dosanjh's Satluj premiered on ZEE5 on July 3, it arrived after three years of battles with India's censorship apparatus. Within 48 hours, it was gone.

The government's Information and Broadcasting Ministry ordered the film's removal, citing national security concerns and alleging that it had bypassed the mandatory Central Board of Film Certification process. The film had originally been submitted under the title Punjab 95 and faced demands for nearly 100 cuts. Rather than comply, the makers pivoted to a direct OTT release under the new title, sidestepping the CBFC entirely since streaming platforms in India do not require theatrical certification.

A Film About Memory, Silenced

Satluj, directed by Honey Trehan, tells the story of Jaswant Singh Khalra, a Punjab-based human rights activist who documented thousands of extrajudicial killings during the state's militancy era in the 1990s. Khalra was abducted by police in 1995 and murdered. His case became a landmark in India's human rights history.

Dosanjh, according to director Trehan, charged just Re 1 for the role. "How can I charge to play someone like Khalra?" the actor reportedly told the team.

The film received an overwhelming audience response during its brief window on ZEE5. When it vanished, Dosanjh went live on Instagram, where fans flooded the comments saying they had already downloaded the film. "We've been fighting to get this film released for the last three to four years," Dosanjh said. "We fought this battle ourselves."

Industry Splits Over Response

The ban has divided Bollywood. Filmmaker Anurag Kashyap publicly accused CBFC chief Prasoon Joshi of raising objections without even watching the film. Actor Tillotama Shome, speaking to Bollywood Hungama, argued that "as a democracy, we should be able to watch all kinds of cinema."

But veteran actor Annu Kapoor pushed back, supporting the government's decision and urging the filmmakers to take their case to the Supreme Court rather than seek public sympathy. "There is a proper channel to follow, isn't there?" he said in an interview. "What's the point of crying about it?"

"If the Censor Board does not grant it a certificate, you should go to the Supreme Court. You acted in the film, and the rules clearly state that."

— Annu Kapoor, actor

Legal Challenges Stall

A law student and ZEE5 subscriber, Sharwan Singh, filed a public interest litigation in the Punjab and Haryana High Court seeking restoration of the film, arguing that its removal curtailed the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). However, the court declined to hear the PIL, noting that neither the producers nor ZEE5 had challenged the ban themselves. The bench did remark that it was "not averse to judicial review," leaving a narrow path open for a future challenge.

ZEE5 issued a statement saying it stood "firmly behind the film and its creative vision" and was exploring "every appropriate avenue through due process" to bring Satluj back. The platform urged viewers not to pirate the film.

The Chilling Effect

The Satluj episode lands at a moment when India's creative class is already navigating an increasingly restrictive environment. Reports indicate the Centre may now push to make CBFC certification mandatory even for direct OTT releases, a move that would fundamentally reshape India's streaming landscape.

For filmmakers in India and the diaspora watching from abroad, the message has grown harder to ignore. Community screenings of Satluj at gurudwaras across five states have continued despite the ban, turning the film into a symbol of resistance against what many see as the state's overreach into artistic expression.

What's Next

The Inter-Departmental Committee set up by the government to review Satluj's content is expected to submit its assessment in the coming weeks. Whether the filmmakers or ZEE5 file a formal legal challenge remains to be seen. Meanwhile, the broader question — how far India's government will go to control what its citizens can watch — hangs unanswered.
